content_metadata.description: This video demonstrates the transesterification process, a crucial step in biodiesel production, conducted by a student and their instructor, highlighting chemical reactions and products.

qAndA.question: What is the name of the student assisting the instructor?
What two chemicals are mixed with the oil to initiate transesterification?
After shaking the mixture, how many distinct layers are visible in the settled solution?

qAndA.answer: Methyl esters or fatty acid methyl esters (FAME).
qAndA.question: What is the scientific term for the biodiesel product formed in the top layer?

qAndA.answer: Manufacturing of cosmetics, soaps, or other products.
qAndA.question: What is one application for the glycerol byproduct found in the bottom layer?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Okay, so to join us for part two, now that we have our completed oil, is a student from
our sustainability and renewable energy systems major.
Hello, I'm David Sabaki.
And he's going to walk us through the trans-estrification process.
So we have some methanol here, methanol, and of course what else do we need?
Our catalyst, so our catalyst is methanol and potassium hydroxide.
And here we have our oil and what are we going to do?
We're going to mix these two together, separate those triglycerides.
So take the oil and pour it into here.
And then we have to vigorously shake it for about ten minutes.
So it looks a little bubbly and the oil hasn't really mixed yet, but once you shake it, you
see that immediate reaction happen.
And then we're going to shake that for about ten minutes and it's going to result in
this mixture here.
And then once we let this mixture wait for a while, some people can choose to let it wait
for a couple hours or overnight, in our case, we have something that looks a little bit
like this.
So what we have here, we've got two layers here, that first layer that we have, this is our
methyl esters, these are our mix of fatty esters or fatty methyl esters, and it's cold.
And right there at that bottom, that slightly darker layer, that is our other product.
So what was the other product that we made when we were doing trans-estrification?
It was glycerol.
So this is the glycerol at the bottom.
And when we go to process this biodiesel now, because actually this part right here,
is methyl esters, this is what we used to make diesel.
This will get filtered out and we'll see in step three, some things that we can do to
it to clean it up.
And this glycerol will be tapped out of the bottom and then used to go in manufacturing
of cosmetics and soaps and a whole other products.

youtube_description:
IPREFER research collaborator and University of Wisconsin-Platteville professor Dr. Pamela Tas presents a brief introductory talk on biodiesel transesterification. This video is the second of a three-part series.  The material is intended for advanced high school and college students interested in ag-based biofuels. The IPREFER research project has a goal of commercially launching pennycress as a cash cover crop in 2021. 

Can you please help our project by completing this brief evaluation at https://illinoisstate.az1.qualtrics.com/jfe/form/SV_0kZgGW4c6kC72nz

 You can learn more about IPREFER at https://www.iprefercap.org. IPREFER is supported by Agriculture and Food Research Initiative Competitive Grant No. 2019-69012-29851 from the National Institute of Food and Agriculture.
